query: When should we use Callaway & Sant’Anna or Sun & Abraham corrections for staggered DiD rather than switching to synthetic control, RD, or IV approaches?

response.query: When should we use Callaway & Sant’Anna or Sun & Abraham corrections for staggered DiD rather than switching to synthetic control, RD, or IV approaches?
response.answer: Use Callaway & Sant’Anna or Sun & Abraham corrections for staggered DiD when treatment effect heterogeneity is present. Synthetic control or RD/IV approaches are preferable when these corrections are insufficient or when data is extensive.

results.content: As the authors note, this is an alternative to a baseline TWFE DiD estimate, but “uses a more stringent criteria for admissable control groups, and is more robust to possible problems with a staggered treatment design in the presence of heterogeneous treatment eﬀects.” By stacking and aligning events in event-time, this approach is equivalent to a setting where the events happen contemporaneously, and it prevents using past treated units as controls, which may occur with a staggered design. The stacked regression approach generates estimates that are slightly biased above the true treatment eﬀect average, which is likely a result of using OLS variance-weighting rather than weighting explicitly by the sample share as in Callaway and Sant’Anna (2020) 21 and Sun and Abraham (2020).15 The results of this stylized simulation show how in settings with panel data and heterogeneous treatment eﬀects that vary through time, the simple TWFE DiD estimate will be biased.

results.title: Synthetic difference-in-differences estimation with staggered treatment timing - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Synthetic difference-in-differences estimation with staggered treatment timing. This note formalizes the synthetic difference-in-differences estimator for staggered treatment adoption settings, as briefly described in Arkhangelsky et al. I compare the estimators obtained using SynthDiD, TWFE, the group time average treatment effect estimator of Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), and the partially pooled synthetic control method estimator of Ben-Michael et al. I find that in this staggered treatment setting, SynthDiD provides a numerically different estimate of the average treatment effect. SynthDiD does this by introducing the weighting of both pre-treatment time periods and cross-sectional units in the construction of a synthetic counterfactual for causal estimation. To illustrate this estimator’s importance and distinction, I employ data from Abrams, 2012a, Abrams, 2012b to demonstrate the differences in estimators obtained through SynthDiD, a standard two-way fixed effects DiD estimator, the group-time average treatment effect estimator of Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), and the partially pooled synthetic control method estimator of Ben-Michael et al. This paper is meant to serve as an introduction to the use of SynthDiD estimation in the staggered treatment timing settings often encountered in empirical research. To demonstrate the use of the staggered-treatment timing synthetic difference-in-differences estimator, replication data from Abrams, 2012a, Abrams, 2012b are used to estimate the causal impact of a law adopted by different states in different years. This estimation is done with a typical two-way fixed effects OLS estimator (TWFE), the synthetic difference-in-differences estimator presented here, the partially-pooled synthetic control estimator of Ben-Michael et al. In this note, I have formalized the functional form of the SynthDiD estimator in settings with staggered treatment timing and have demonstrated its practical use. While, the brief empirical demonstration is in no way meant to be a robust replication of Abrams, 2012a, Abrams, 2012b, it does demonstrate that different aggregated average treatment effect estimates can be obtained using this new and arguably more precise estimator. ### Synthetic control methods for comparative case studies: Estimating the effect of California’s tobacco control program. This estimator, as extended to staggered treatment adoption settings in Porreca (2022), allows for a localized causal estimator in which treated units are compared to a never treated control group that is weighted on both the time and unit dimensions.
